name: Least Astonishment and Interface Design
intent: Design functions and APIs so that a caller who guesses from the names, the types and the usual conventions guesses right, and make the dangerous thing hard to do by accident.
scenario: A team's helper library has delete(path), which removes a directory and everything under it by default; get_user(name), which creates the user if it is missing; export(rows, true, false), whose two booleans can be swapped without any error; and get_sorted(list), which sorts the caller's list in place. Each one does something reasonable, and each has caused an incident, because the caller did what the name suggested and the code did something else.
problem: The principle of least astonishment says an interface should behave the way its users expect. The difficulty is that the author knows how it works, and so cannot easily see what a newcomer will guess. A caller reads names first, then signatures, and documentation last, if at all. Every behaviour that is visible only in the documentation is a trap for those who do not read it. But the cure can be overdone: an interface that forces every option to be spelled out on every call is not safer, it only moves the mistakes to the places people copy and paste from.

howItWorks.title: Think like the caller who reads least
howItWorks.text: Callers differ in how much they read: some look at the name only, some open the signature, some read the documentation. A design that is safe only for the third group is unsafe for most calls, because most calls are written quickly. In the sample, a hurried team of 20 callers makes 73 mistaken calls against a library with four hazards, a careful team 15.

howItWorks.title: Name what it does, including its side effects
howItWorks.text: A name is a promise. get_user that creates a user, or get_sorted that reorders the caller's list, breaks it. Split the behaviours: find_user returns nothing if the user is missing, and ensure_user creates one, so the dangerous act has its own name. Convention matters as well: in Python, list.sort() sorts in place and sorted() returns a new list, and an interface that follows such a convention astonishes nobody.

howItWorks.title: Make the safe thing the default
howItWorks.text: A default is the answer given by every caller who says nothing, so it should be the one that does the least harm. delete(path) that refuses a non-empty directory unless told recursive=true is a small nuisance for the person who meant it, and saves the person who did not: in the sample, 2 files are lost against none. A destructive default is, in the model, the largest single source of damage: 80 of 168 points for a mixed team.

howItWorks.title: Make misuse hard to write
howItWorks.text: Two booleans in a row are easy to swap, and the call export(rows, true, false) says nothing at the call site. Named options, enums or small types make the intent readable in the call and make a swap impossible or visible. The same goes for argument order, units (cents or dollars) and anything where two parameters share a type: let the compiler or the reader notice before production does.

howItWorks.title: Do not buy safety with noise
howItWorks.text: The over-applied extreme is to require every option on every call, with long names and mandatory confirmations. In the model, a call then needs 14 arguments instead of 4. Callers who only read names do not read the prompts either: they paste the confirmation settings from the nearest working example, so for dangerous operations 16 mistaken calls remain with a mixed team. Least astonishment means the common case is short and obvious, and the rare dangerous case is explicit.

pros: Fewer bugs at call sites, because the guess most people make is the right one
Code reviews can see intent from the call without opening the definition
New team members become productive faster, and documentation matters less
Dangerous operations stay deliberate, which limits the damage of a slip
cons: What is surprising depends on the audience: it is a judgement, not a measurement
Splitting behaviours (find, ensure, create) means more functions to learn and keep consistent
Following convention can conflict with a better design, and then something has to give
Changing an existing surprising interface breaks the callers that depend on it
whenToUse: Any public function, library or API that people will call without reading its source
Operations that delete, overwrite, charge or send: make the dangerous version explicit
Parameters of the same type that can be swapped, or flags that change what the call means
whenNotToUse: As a reason to remove all options: a rare, dangerous operation should still be possible, just explicit
For a private helper with one caller, where a long ceremony costs more than it saves
When a convention in the language or the domain differs from your preference: following it astonishes fewer people
pitfalls: Judging by your own expectations: the author always knows how the code works, so test the interface on someone who has not seen it
Booleans as options: two or more in a row are swappable, and a lone true at the call site means nothing
A getter, a property or a query with a side effect, such as creating, caching a change or sending something
A default that is convenient for the author's own use and destructive for everyone else's
Methods that return the same list after mutating it, so callers cannot tell a copy from the original
Inconsistent conventions in one API: copy(dst, src) next to move(src, dst), or one function that throws on a missing item and another that returns null
Fixing a surprising interface by adding a warning to the documentation: the people who bite are those who do not read it
Over-correcting into mandatory confirmations and verbose options, which callers learn to paste past

roles.label: Caller
roles.description: A developer who guesses from names and types, and reads documentation last.

roles.label: Interface
roles.description: The names, parameters and defaults a caller sees.

roles.label: Implementation
roles.description: What the code really does, including side effects.

roles.label: Data
roles.description: Files, users and lists that a mistaken call can change or lose.

quiz.question: delete(path) removes a directory and everything in it by default. A caller who thinks the directory is empty calls it. Which fix addresses the cause?
options: Add a sentence to the documentation saying that the delete is recursive by default.
Rename the recursive parameter to something longer, so that its effect is clearer.
Print a warning after the files are gone, so the caller can restore them.
Make the default refuse a non-empty directory unless recursive=true is passed.
quiz.explanation: The default is what every caller who says nothing gets, so it should do the least harm. Documentation and after-the-fact warnings only help people who read them, and the people who are hurt mostly do not.

quiz.question: A function get_user(name) creates the user if it does not exist. A caller writes: if get_user(name) is not None, then the user exists. What is wrong?
options: The name suggests a read but it writes, so the check always passes.
The caller should have wrapped the check in a database transaction, to be safe.
None is the wrong value to compare against here, and an empty string should be used instead.
Nothing is wrong: functions that create on demand are always the safest design.
quiz.explanation: A hidden side effect makes the name lie. Split the behaviours: find_user reads and may return nothing, ensure_user creates, and each name says what it does.

quiz.question: A team makes an API 'safe' by requiring 14 arguments on every call, including confirmations. What is the likely result for callers who skim?
options: They read all 14 arguments carefully, so the dangerous cases are all caught.
They paste the settings from an example that worked, so the confirmations stop meaning anything.
They stop using the API, because documentation is then unnecessary.
They get the same result as with a safe default, with extra typing as the only cost.
quiz.explanation: Callers who read names only do not read prompts either. Ceremony on every call gets copied past, so the dangerous case is no safer. Keep the common case short, and make only the rare dangerous case explicit.
